notes.angle: Lonewolf mang lại giải pháp máy chủ chat XMPP độc lập viết bằng Rust chỉ với một binary duy nhất và database nhúng redb, cắt giảm toàn bộ sự cồng kềnh của ejabberd hay Prosody.

facts.fact: Lonewolf là một máy chủ XMPP tự host viết bằng Rust, được cấp phép mã nguồn mở theo giấy phép Apache-2.0.
facts.quote: Lonewolf is a self-hosted [XMPP](https://xmpp.org/) server written in Rust.

facts.fact: Máy chủ đóng gói trong một binary duy nhất với bộ lưu trữ nhúng, cấu hình chạy thử nghiệm chỉ cần 2 dòng toml.
facts.quote: One binary with embedded storage. There's no database server to install, and a local test server needs two lines of config.

facts.fact: Lonewolf lưu trữ dữ liệu tài khoản và tin nhắn bằng redb - một cơ sở dữ liệu key-value nhúng thuần Rust.
facts.quote: keeps everything in an embedded [redb](https://github.com/cberner/redb) database.

facts.fact: Hệ thống lưu trữ redb hỗ trợ ACID đầy đủ và dựa trên B+tree sao chép khi ghi (copy-on-write).
facts.quote: redb is written in pure Rust and is loosely inspired by lmdb. Data is stored in a collection of copy-on-write B+trees.

facts.fact: Phiên bản mới nhất v0.3.0 bổ sung tính năng federation, cho phép trao đổi tin nhắn và presence với các server XMPP khác.
facts.quote: The big one in this release is federation: Lonewolf can now talk to other XMPP servers.

facts.fact: Tính năng liên thông federation của Lonewolf chỉ xác thực qua chứng chỉ TLS và SASL EXTERNAL, không hỗ trợ Server Dialback.
facts.quote: Lonewolf authenticates peers by certificate only. The other server needs a trusted certificate and SASL EXTERNAL support. We don't support Server Dialback.

facts.fact: Lonewolf hỗ trợ Direct TLS theo chuẩn XEP-0368 bên cạnh STARTTLS truyền thống trên cổng chuyên biệt.
facts.quote: Clients and servers can now connect with TLS from the first byte (XEP-0368), using new dedicated listeners.

facts.fact: Hỗ trợ tích hợp tự động cấp và gia hạn chứng chỉ Let's Encrypt qua giao thức ACME HTTP-01 chỉ với 1 dòng cấu hình.
Lonewolf hỗ trợ đồng bộ bản sao tin nhắn đa thiết bị thông qua chuẩn Carbons (XEP-0280) và Stanza Forwarding (XEP-0297).
facts.quote: Message Carbons (XEP-0280) lets clients enable sent and received message copies for each session. Stanza Forwarding (XEP-0297) supplies the copy envelopes.

facts.fact: Prosody được viết bằng Lua, cung cấp Docker image chính thức trên nền Debian 13 (trixie) và quản lý qua prosodyctl.
facts.quote: Docker images are built off an __Debian 13 (trixie)__ base.

facts.fact: ejabberd được viết bằng Erlang và yêu cầu cài đặt Erlang/OTP, Libexpat, OpenSSL, Zlib cùng các thư viện cơ sở dữ liệu nếu biên dịch từ source.
facts.quote: To compile ejabberd you need: - GNU Make - GCC - Libexpat 1.95 or higher - Erlang/OTP R10B-9 or higher.

caveats: Lonewolf đang ở giai đoạn pre-1.0; định dạng lưu trữ, cấu hình và interface có thể thay đổi trước khi ra bản ổn định.
Hiện tại máy chủ chỉ chạy dạng single-node; tính năng clustering và PostgreSQL storage nằm ở lộ trình sau.
Chưa hỗ trợ phòng chat nhóm (MUC), upload file qua HTTP, lưu trữ lịch sử tin nhắn (MAM), và Stream Management.
Federation chỉ chấp nhận server đối tác có chứng chỉ TLS hợp lệ và SASL EXTERNAL, hoàn toàn không hỗ trợ Server Dialback.
Tài khoản hoặc mật khẩu cập nhật trên v0.3.0 lưu định dạng credential mà v0.2.0 không đọc được, khiến việc rollback gặp khó khăn.
Let's Encrypt yêu cầu mở cổng 80 công khai để xác thực tên miền qua ACME HTTP-01.
gaps: Mức tiêu thụ RAM và CPU thực tế khi chạy ở trạng thái nghỉ và khi chịu tải bao nhiêu MB?
Có sẵn Docker image chính thức dựng sẵn trên Docker Hub / GitHub Container Registry hay bắt buộc phải compile từ source bằng Rust?
Hiệu năng chịu tải khi so sánh trực tiếp benchmark giữa Lonewolf với Prosody và ejabberd trên cùng một cấu hình phần cứng VPS?

## lonewolf-im/lonewolf (https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf)
Description: XMPP with teeth 🐺
Homepage: -
Language: Rust; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-09-17; last push 2026-11-19
Latest release: v0.3.0 (2026-11-13)
README (start):
Lonewolf: XMPP with teeth.

  

[](https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf/actions)
[](https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf/releases)
[](https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf/blob/main/LICENSE)

Lonewolf is a self-hosted [XMPP](https://xmpp.org/) server written in Rust. It's
meant to be easy to set up, cheap to run, and able to grow into a cluster when you
need one.

> [!NOTE]
> Lonewolf is early, pre-1.0 software. It hosts chat on your domains and
> federates with other XMPP servers through certificate-authenticated TLS.
> Clustering comes later.
>
> Most of Lonewolf's code, tests and docs are written with AI coding agents. The
> maintainer sets the design and scope and reviews the changes.

## Why Lonewolf?

- **Easy to run.** One binary with embedded storage. There's no database server
  to install, and a local test server needs two lines of config.
- **Light on resources.** It's native Rust and frugal with memory and CPU.
- **Standards first.** It follows the core XMPP RFCs closely, so standard
  clients behave the way you'd expect.
- **Limits you can see.** Connections, stanzas, rates and resources all have
  configurable limits, so one misbehaving client can't take your server down.

## What works today

- Chat on your hosted domains and with users on other XMPP servers, with several
  devices per account
- Contact lists, presence subscriptions, and offline messages that keep their
  original timestamps
- Message copies across your devices (Carbons), service discovery, vCard
  profiles, ping, software version queries and private client settings
- STARTTLS and direct TLS, SCRAM login with channel binding, and optional
  client-certificate login
- TLS certificates from your own files or from Let's Encrypt
- Account management with `lonewolfctl`, Prometheus metrics, structured logs and
  graceful shutdown

Lonewolf runs on Unix-like systems, and CI tests it on Linux and macOS. The
[standards reference](docs/STANDARDS.md) lists every supported XEP and RFC, and
its limits.

## What's next

The [roadmap to 1.0](docs/ROADMAP.md) covers, in order:

1. External components, group chats, file upload and the rest of basic desktop IM
2. Message archives, Stream Management, blocking, avatars and bookmarks
3. PostgreSQL storage and clustering
4. Mobile and web support

## Quick start

Let's get a server running on your machine and send a message between two
accounts. It only takes a few minutes, plus however long your first Rust build
takes.

You'll need Linux or macOS, Git, a [stable Rust toolchain](https://rust-lang.org/tools/install/),
a system linker, and an [XMPP client](https://xmpp.org/software/) to chat with.

### 1. Build it

```sh
git clone --branch v0.3.0 https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf.git
cd lonewolf
cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl
```

You'll end up with two binaries in `target/release/`: `lonewolf`, the server, and
`lonewolfctl`, a small tool for managing accounts.

### 2. Start the server

Create a `lonewolf.toml` in the repo root with a single listener:

```toml
[[c2s.listeners]]
address = "127.0.0.1:5222"
```

Then start it:

```sh
./target/release/lonewolf --config ./lonewolf.toml
```

That's all the config you need. Lonewolf listens on your loopback address only,
serves the built-in `localhost` domain with its default features, and keeps
everything in an embedded [redb](https://github.com/cberner/redb) database. Leave
it running.

### 3. Create two accounts

In a second terminal, from the same directory:

```sh
./target/release/lonewolfctl account create alice@localhost
./target/release/lonewolfctl account create bob@localhost
./target/release/lonewolfctl account list
```

You'll be asked to choose a password for each account. Addresses like
`alice@localhost` are called JIDs, short for Jabber IDs.

### 4. Say hello

Sign in as both users, using two clients or two accounts in one client, with
these settings:

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Account | `alice@localhost` or `bob@localhost` |
| Password | The one you just chose |
| Server address override | `127.0.0.1` |
| Port | `5222` |
| Connection security | STARTTLS, required |

The server creates a self-signed certificate for `localhost` when it starts, so
your client will ask whether to trust it. Say yes for this test. You'll get a new
certificate each time the server restarts, unless you give Lonewolf your own.

Now add `bob@localhost` as a contact from Alice's account, and accept the request
on Bob's side. You should see each other come online and be able to chat.

Want to see offline delivery? Sign Bob out and send him a message. He'll get it,
with its original timestamp, the next time he signs in.

When you're done, press `Ctrl+C` to stop the server. Your accounts and any
undelivered messages are saved in `./data/lonewolf.dat`.

## Configuration

Lonewolf reads `./lonewolf.toml` if it exists and uses built-in defaults
otherwise. If you pass `--config`, that file has to exist.

[`examples/lonewolf.toml`](examples/lonewolf.toml) documents every setting and its
default. Everything in it is commented out, so you only uncomment what you want
to change.

### Hosting your own domain

To serve a real domain, give Lonewolf a certificate for it:

```toml
[hosts."example.com".tls]
certificate_chain_path = "./certs/example.com.crt"
private_key_path = "./certs/example.com.key"

[[c2s.listeners]]
address = "0.0.0.0:5222"
```

This replaces the default `localhost` host with `example.com` and listens on all
IPv4 interfaces. Relative paths are resolved from the directory you start the
server in.

### Let's Encrypt

To have Lonewolf get and renew the certificate for you, replace the file paths
with one line. You can choose this per host.

```toml
[hosts."example.com".tls]
provider = "letsencrypt"
```

This accepts Let's Encrypt's subscriber terms. Let's Encrypt checks that you
control the domain by connecting to port 80 on each of its public addresses, so
that port has to reach Lonewolf. If a proxy already owns port 80, have it forward
to a local port, keeping the original Host header and path:

```toml
[letsencrypt]
listen = ["127.0.0.1:8080"]
```

The certificates and ACME account live in `./data/lonewolf/acme.redb`, so keep it
on durable storage. To test against Let's Encrypt's staging server first, see
`directory_url` in the config reference.

Running behind a web proxy or in a container? The [deployment guide](docs/DEPLOYMENT.md)
covers ports, DNS, proxy setup, container permissions and common errors.

## Managing accounts

`lonewolfctl` talks to the running server over a local Unix socket, which is
`./run/lonewolf/admin.sock` by default. Anyone who can open that socket can
manage accounts, so restrict its file permissions.

```sh
./target/release/lonewolfctl account list
./target/release/lonewolfctl account get alice@localhost
./target/release/lonewolfctl account password alice@localhost
./target/release/lonewolfctl account delete bob@localhost
```

Changing a password prompts for the new one twice, and deleting an account asks
you to confirm first. A few handy flags:

- `--socket PATH` for when the server uses a different socket, or you're running
  the tool from another directory
- `--json` for machine-readable output
- `--password-stdin` to read the password from standard input, for scripting
  `create` and `password`

## Contributing

Found a bug or have an idea? [Open an issue](https://github.com/lonewolf-im/lonewolf/issues).
For bug reports, it helps to include the commit you built, your platform, the
relevant config, and steps to reproduce. Please strip out passwords and private
messages first.

Found a security problem? Please report it privately instead; see
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

Thinking about a new feature? Check the [roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md) first. It may
already be planned, and it helps us figure out where the feature fits.

## Contact
If you have any suggestion or question:

JID: [ortuman@lonewolf-im.com](xmpp:ortuman@lonewolf-im.com)

## License

Lonewolf is licensed under [Apache-2.0](LICENSE).

## prosody/prosody-docker (https://github.com/prosody/prosody-docker)
Description: Docker image building system for the Prosody XMPP server
Homepage: https://hub.docker.com/r/prosodyim/prosody
Language: Lua; license: none; created 2014-11-13; last push 2026-11-07
Latest release: 1.4.2 (2016-03-11)
README (start):
# Docker build scripts for Prosody build server

This is the Prosody Docker image building repository. It is used by our build server to build and publish Docker images for stable releases and nightly builds.

## Published images

- **[Docker Hub image prosodyim/prosody](https://hub.docker.com/r/prosodyim/prosody): official images, up-to-date, automated builds.**
- ~~[Docker Hub image prosody/prosody](https://hub.docker.com/r/prosody/prosody)~~: official images, outdated, manual builds.

## Running

It works by enabling the [prosody package repository](https://prosody.im/download/package_repository) and installing the selected Prosody package from there based on the `PROSODY_PACKAGE` build argument.

Docker images are built off an __Debian 13 (trixie)__ base.

```bash
docker run -d --name prosody -p 5222:5222 prosody/prosody
```

A user can be created by using environment variables `LOCAL`, `DOMAIN`, and `PASSWORD`. This performs the following action on startup:

  prosodyctl register *local* *domain* *password*

Any error from this script is ignored. Prosody will not check the user exists before running the command (i.e. existing users will be overwritten). It is expected that [mod_admin_adhoc](http://prosody.im/doc/modules/mod_admin_adhoc) will then be in place for managing users (and the server).

### Ports

The image exposes the following ports to the docker host:

* __80__: HTTP port
* __443__: HTTPS port
* __5222__: c2s port
* __5269__: s2s port
* __5347__: XMPP component port
* __5280__: BOSH / websocket port
* __5281__: Secure BOSH / websocket port

Note: These default ports can be changed in your configuration file. Therefore if you change these ports will not be exposed.

### Volumes

Volumes can be mounted at the following locations for adding in files:

* __/etc/prosody__:
  * Prosody configuration file(s)
* __/etc/prosody/certs__:
  * SSL certificates
* __/etc/prosody/modules__:
  * Location for including additional modules
* __/var/lib/prosody__:
  * Location of data

### Environment Variables

* `DOMAIN`, `LOCAL`, `PASSWORD` - These three are used by `entrypoint.sh` to create an initial account `$LOCAL@$DOMAIN` with `$PASSWORD` as password.
* `PROSODY_PLUGIN_PATHS` - Comma-separated list of additional paths to search for plugins. Defaults to `/etc/prosody/modules`.
* `PROSODY_ADMINS` - Comma-separated list of user addresses treated as admins.
* `PROSODY_ENABLE_MODULES` - Comma-separated list of additional plugins to load.
* `PROSODY_DISABLE_MODULES` - Comma-separated list of modules to disable, e.g. for auto-enabled modules.
* `PROSODY_TURN_HOST` - Hostname of TURN server
* `PROSODY_TURN_PORT` - Port number of TURN server
* `PROSODY_TURN_SECRET` - Shared secret for TURN
* `PROSODY_TURN_TLS_PORT` -  Port number for STUN over TLS
* `PROSODY_RETENTION_DAYS` - How many days worth of message archives and shared file to keep.
* `PROSODY_DNS_RESOLVERS` - Comma-separated list of DNS resolvers to use instead of what `/etc/resolv.conf` points to.
* `PROSODY_USE_DANE` - Whether to enable [DANE](https://prosody.im/doc/dane) (requires [DNSSEC](https://prosody.im/doc/dnssec) aware resolvers).
* `PROSODY_S2S_SECURE_AUTH` - Whether to require that remote servers present valid certificates. Enabled by default.
* `PROSODY_C2S_RATE_LIMIT` - Rate limit for client-to-server connections. Defaults to `10kb/s`.
* `PROSODY_S2S_RATE_LIMIT` - Rate limit for server-to-server connections. Defaults to `30kb/s`.
* `PROSODY_STORAGE` - [Storage driver](https://prosody.im/doc/storage) to use. Defaults to `internal`.
* `PROSODY_SQL_DRIVER` - One of `SQLite3`, `PostgreSQL` or `MySQL`. Selects SQL backend when `PROSODY_STORAGE` is set to `sql`.
* `PROSODY_SQL_DB` - Name of SQL database to use.
* `PROSODY_SQL_HOST` - Hostname of SQL database to connect to (PostgreSQL and MySQL only).
* `PROSODY_SQL_USERNAME`, `PROSODY_SQL_PASSWORD` - Credentials for connecting to SQL database.
* `PROSODY_ARCHIVE_EXPIRY_DAYS` - When set, overrides `PROSODY_RETENTION_DAYS` for message archives.
* `PROSODY_LOGLEVEL` - Log level, one of `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. Defaults to `info`.
* `PROSODY_STATISTICS` - [Statistics provider](https://prosody.im/doc/statistics) to use, e.g. `internal`. Default disabled.
* `PROSODY_STATISTICS_INTERVAL` - Statistics collection interval. A number or the string `manual` for OpenMetrics-triggered collection. Defaults to `60`.
* `PROSODY_CERTIFICATES` - Path to TLS certificates and private keys, relative to the config file. Defaults to `certs`, i.e.
* `PROSODY_VIRTUAL_HOSTS` - Comma-separated list of domain names to initialize as hosts that provide user accounts. Defaults to the hostname of the container. `/etc/prosody/certs`.
* `PROSODY_NETWORK_HOSTNAME` - Public domain name for use with e.g. HTTP. Defaults to the first entry in `PROSODY_VIRTUAL_HOSTS`.
* `PROSODY_COMPONENTS` - Comma-separated list of _internal_ components in the form `name.example.com:type` where `type` can be e.g. `muc`, `http_file_share`.
* `PROSODY_MUC_MODULES` - Comma-separated list of additional modules to enable on a MUC component.
* `PROSODY_UPLOAD_EXPIRY_DAYS` - When set, overrides `PROSODY_RETENTION_DAYS` for uploaded files.
* `PROSODY_UPLOAD_LIMIT_MB` - Size limit in MiB for individual uploaded files.
* `PROSODY_UPLOAD_STORAGE_GB` - Total amount of storage available for file uploads.
* `PROSODY_EXTERNAL_COMPONENTS` - Comma-separated list of _external_ components, in the form of `name.example.com:secret`.
* `PROSODY_COMPONENT_SECRET` - Component shared secret if not provided as part of `PROSODY_EXTERNAL_COMPONENTS`.
* `PROSODY_EXTRA_CONFIG` - Path to additional configuration file. Can contain wildcards. Defaults to `/etc/prosody/conf.d/*.cfg.lua`.

### Example

```bash
docker run -it \
   -p 5222:5222 \
   -p 5269:5269 \
   -e LOCAL=romeo \
   -e DOMAIN=shakespeare.lit \
   -e PASSWORD=juliet4ever \
   -v /data/prosody/configuration:/etc/prosody \
   -v /logs/prosody:/var/log/prosody \
   -v /data/prosody/modules:/usr/lib/prosody-modules \
   prosody/prosody:0.12
```

## Building

```bash
docker build --build-arg PROSODY_PACKAGE=prosody-0.12 -t prosody/prosody:0.12 .
```

## Alternative Dockerfiles

There are many alternative Dockerfiles for Prosody available if this one
does not suit your needs:

  - [OpusVL/prosody-docker](https://github.com/OpusVL/prosody-docker/)
  - [unclev/prosody-docker-extended](https://github.com/unclev/prosody-docker-extended)

## mikma/ejabberd (https://github.com/mikma/ejabberd)
Description: Fork of processone/ejabberd-oldsvn. Robust and scalable Jabber / XMPP Instant Messaging platform 
Homepage: http://www.process-one.net/en/ejabberd/
Language: Erlang; license: NOASSERTION; created 2009-07-13; last push 2009-12-31
No releases
README (start):
ejabberd - High-Performance Enterprise Instant Messaging Server 

Quickstart guide

0. Requirements

To compile ejabberd you need:
 - GNU Make
 - GCC
 - Libexpat 1.95 or higher
 - Erlang/OTP R10B-9 or higher. The recommended version is R12B-5.
   Support for R13 is experimental.
 - OpenSSL 0.9.6 or higher, for STARTTLS, SASL and SSL
   encryption. Optional, highly recommended.
 - Zlib 1.2.3 or higher, for Stream Compression support
   (XEP-0138). Optional.
 - Erlang mysql library. Optional. MySQL authentication/storage.
 - Erlang pgsql library. Optional. PostgreSQL authentication/storage.
 - PAM library. Optional. For Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM).
 - GNU Iconv 1.8 or higher, for the IRC Transport
   (mod_irc). Optional. Not needed on systems with GNU Libc.
 - ImageMagick’s Convert program. Optional. For CAPTCHA challenges.
 - exmpp 0.9.1 or higher. Optional. For import/export XEP-0227 files. 

1. Compile and install on *nix systems

To compile ejabberd, go to the directory src/ and execute the commands:
  ./configure
  make

To install ejabberd, run this command with system administrator rights
(root user):

  sudo make install

These commands will:
 - Install the configuration files in /etc/ejabberd/
 - Install ejabberd binary, header and runtime files in /lib/ejabberd/
 - Install the administration script: /sbin/ejabberdctl
 - Install ejabberd documentation in /share/doc/ejabberd/
 - Create a spool directory: /var/lib/ejabberd/
 - Create a directory for log files: /var/log/ejabberd/

2. Start ejabberd

You can use the ejabberdctl command line administration script to
start and stop ejabberd. For example:
  ejabberdctl start

For detailed information please refer to the
ejabberd Installation and Operation Guide

 ortuman released this 
 v0.3.0
 784ad60 

The big one in this release is federation: Lonewolf can now talk to other XMPP servers. We also added direct TLS and a handful of extensions that desktop clients rely on.

Lonewolf is still pre-1.0 and runs as a single node. Full XMPP compliance and clustering are on the roadmap.

What's new
Federation

Your users can now exchange messages, presence, IQs, and roster subscriptions with people on other XMPP servers. If a host has a certificate and a public DNS name, federation is on by default, with nothing extra to configure.

Lonewolf authenticates peers by certificate only. The other server needs a trusted certificate and SASL EXTERNAL support. We don't support Server Dialback.

When the other server supports it, both directions share a single connection (XEP-0288). Servers also tell each other their stanza size and idle limits up front (XEP-0478).

Federation checks certificate revocation lists published by the CA, fetched over plain HTTP. If a CRL can't be downloaded, the connection goes ahead anyway. You can turn downloads off with s2s.tls.fetch_crls = false, or point s2s.tls.crls_path at a local file to use only that.

Direct TLS

Clients and servers can now connect with TLS from the first byte (XEP-0368), using new dedicated listeners. Outbound federation discovers both STARTTLS and direct TLS endpoints.

More for desktop clients
Private XML Storage (XEP-0049) gives clients a place to keep private settings and legacy bookmarks.
Software Version (XEP-0092) answers "what server is this?" queries. It doesn't reveal the operating system unless you turn that on.

Both are enabled by default.

Short-lived certificates

Use letsencrypt.certificate_profile to pick one of the profiles your CA advertises, including short-lived certificates. If you change the profile, Lonewolf renews early so the new one takes effect right away.

SCRAM-SHA-512 (opt-in)

You can now enable SCRAM-SHA-512 and SCRAM-SHA-512-PLUS. Be aware that they come from an expired Internet-Draft, not an RFC, and aren't registered with IANA.

Even if you leave SHA-512 login disabled, new accounts and password changes now store credentials that v0.2.0 can't read, so rolling back isn't straightforward.

See the standards reference for exactly what's supported and the configuration reference for every setting and its default.

cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl -p lonewolfbench

The benchmark tool is now called lonewolfbench instead of lonewolf-bench, so update any scripts that call it. All you need is a stable Rust toolchain and a system linker on Linux or macOS. The quick start walks you through setup.

Lonewolf v0.2.0 adds discovery, account profiles, and message synchronization for local XMPP clients. It remains a pre-1.0 server for accounts on the domains you host. Federation and full XMPP compliance remain on the roadmap.

Client features
Service Discovery (XEP-0030) answers information and items queries for served domains and local accounts, with resource visibility based on authorization.
vcard-temp (XEP-0054) stores account profiles across restarts. Owners replace their profiles; authenticated local users can retrieve them, including when the owner is offline. Account deletion also deletes its vCard.
XMPP Ping (XEP-0199) answers eligible server and account pings. It does not send proactive heartbeats.
Message Carbons (XEP-0280) lets clients enable sent and received message copies for each session. Stanza Forwarding (XEP-0297) supplies the copy envelopes. Clients must enable Carbons again after reconnecting.

The standards reference records the reviewed revisions, supported roles, limits, and verification evidence. Stanza Forwarding support is limited to Carbons copies; this release does not add message archives, stream resumption, or avatar synchronization.

Operations and tooling
The server reports readiness and bound C2S and metrics addresses through NOTIFY_SOCKET for service managers.
Accepted C2S connections use TCP_NODELAY to send small writes without Nagle delays.
The new lonewolf-bench tool measures idle connections, message delivery, and connection churn against local or remote servers. It records run artifacts and compares compatible runs.
Stanza errors include explanatory text. A cancelled stanza flush preserves the stream-error reply path.
Dependencies were updated. Tests use explicit synchronization, and nightly CI checks for flaky tests.

redb

    

A simple, portable, high-performance, ACID, embedded key-value store.

redb is written in pure Rust and is loosely inspired by lmdb. Data is stored in a collection of copy-on-write B+trees. For more details, see the design doc

use redb::{Database, Error, ReadableDatabase, ReadableTable, TableDefinition};

const TABLE: TableDefinition<&str, u64> = TableDefinition::new("my_data");

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let db = Database::create("my_db.redb")?;
    let write_txn = db.begin_write()?;
    {
        let mut table = write_txn.open_table(TABLE)?;
        table.insert("my_key", &123)?;
    }
    write_txn.commit()?;

    let read_txn = db.begin_read()?;
    let table = read_txn.open_table(TABLE)?;
    assert_eq!(table.get("my_key")?.unwrap().value(), 123);

    Ok(())
}
Status

Stable and maintained.

The file format is stable, and a reasonable effort will be made to provide an upgrade path if there are any future changes to it.

Features
Zero-copy, thread-safe, BTreeMap based API
Fully ACID-compliant transactions
MVCC support for concurrent readers & writer, without blocking
Crash-safe by default
Savepoints and rollbacks
Multi-process access to one database, with a single or several writer processes
no_std

Turning off the std feature builds redb without the standard library. It needs alloc, panic = "abort", and a target with atomic compare-and-swap -- Cortex-M3 and above, but not Cortex-M0. Embedded targets abort on panic by default. Tests always unwind, so tests run on the host need the std feature, which a dev-dependency on redb can enable. There is no filesystem, so storage is supplied by implementing StorageBackend, which reports failures with BackendError::Other, and passing it to Builder::create_with_backend() or Builder::open_read_only_with_backend(). The uuid feature requires std, and cache_metrics requires a target with 64-bit atomics.

Development

just and rootless podman are required. Toolchain setup, dependency vendoring, and cargo-deny checks may use network access without compiling project dependencies. Other development recipes continue to run on the host. Cargo build artifacts are cached in the redb-sandbox-target Podman volume; remove that volume to force a clean sandbox build.

Benchmarks

redb has similar performance to other top embedded key-value stores such as lmdb and rocksdb
